old: Its name may trace back to a single ancient Semitic root that named this animal thousands of years before English existed.
The English word for this desert animal passed through Greek and Latin before landing in French and then English.
It's a cousin of Arabic jamal and Hebrew gamál — same root, different alphabets.
clues: This large domesticated animal has a name that barely changed in sound or meaning as it traveled from an ancient Semitic root into Greek, Latin, French and English.
A humped beast that carries riders and cargo across desert sands, going long stretches without water. It is far bigger than its South American cousin, the llama.
Arabic calls it jamal and Hebrew calls it gamál, and English has a famous saying about the final straw that breaks its back.
